Valve stage lab: triode vs pentode saturation, bias and antialiasing

Ohm (analog-modelling research notes) · generated 2026-10-18 23:41 CEST · research toward a saturator inspired by the Thermionic Culture Vulture. Nothing here is measured from, or claimed to match, the original unit.

In one paragraph. I built a small NumPy lab that solves a single common-cathode valve stage with published valve models (Koren triode and pentode, plus the Dempwolf–Zölzer triode), then measured its harmonics and how much different antialiasing schemes help. Three findings matter for the plugin. (1) Bias steers even vs odd harmonics in every model. At moderate drive (1×A10%) and a cold bias (plate at 0.85 B+), even-harmonic energy exceeds odd by 15 to 38 dB. Near a "centre" bias the 2nd harmonic cancels and odd harmonics take over: at 2× drive the most odd-dominant point is 12 to 21 dB odd-over-even, depending on the valve. That is the mechanism we need behind a Culture-Vulture-style bias knob. (2) The pentode stand-in's symmetric, odd-dominant point sits at a hotter bias than the triodes' (Va0 ≈ 0.45–0.50 B+ vs 0.55–0.65), and its gain is about 1.9× the 12AX7's in the same stage. (3) Antialiasing: at 5 kHz and 2× drive, first-order ADAA alone removes 8 dB of aliasing (from -32.0 to -40.1 dB). 2× oversampling plus ADAA1 reaches -76.9 dB, and 4× oversampling reaches -87.5 dB. In scalar C that is about 50 ns vs 85 ns per sample. Either is cheap. The real cost driver is the quality of the oversampling filter, not the oversampling factor.

1. Why this, and what's missing

No public schematic for any Culture Vulture revision exists. Per the manuals and published descriptions, the valves are an EF86 input, a 6AS6 dual-control pentode doing the distortion, and a 5963 output. So before guessing a circuit, I wanted to understand what a single valve stage does to a signal as bias and drive change, using only published valve data, and how to make that alias-free cheaply. Everything below is a single stage with textbook component values, not the unit's circuit.

Stand-ins (important). I found no published model parameters for the 6AS6 or the 5963.
  • 6AS6: modelled with EF86 (Koren-format fit); Koren's own 6AN8P pentode fit is kept in the code as a second reference. No published Koren/other fit found. 6AS6 is a sharp-cutoff dual-control pentode (Tung-Sol data: Va=Vg2=120 V, Vg1=-2 V, Vg3=-3 V, Ia=3.6 mA, gm(g1)=1850 umho, gm(g3)=810 umho). Its suppressor-grid control is NOT modelled by any Koren pentode equation. data sheet
  • 5963: modelled with 12AU7 (Koren). No published fit found. RCA data: medium-mu twin triode, mu=21, rp~6600 ohm, gm=3200 umho at Va=67.5 V, Vg=0, Ia=8.5 mA; widely described as close to 12AU7 near typical bias. data sheet
The 6AS6's defining feature, control from its suppressor grid (g3), is not covered by any Koren pentode equation. Modelling it will need 6AS6 measurements or curves digitised from the data sheet, fitted to a model with a g3 term.

2. Valve models (with every parameter's source)

Koren triode [1] (eq. 4; the factor 2 is Koren's (1+sgn E1) for E1≥0):

E1 = (VP/KP) · ln(1 + exp(KP(1/μ + VG/√(KVB + VP2))))     IP = 2 E1X / KG1

Koren pentode [1] (eq. 5 and eq. 3 with the errata's /μ):

E1 = (VG2/KP) · ln(1 + exp(KP(1/μ + VG1/VG2)))     IP = 2 E1X/KG1 · arctan(VP/KVB)     IG2 = (VG2/μ + VG1)X/KG2

Dempwolf–Zölzer triode [4] (eqs. 10–12), physically motivated, with a fitted grid current:

IK = G [ln(1 + eC(VA/μ + VG))/C]γ    IG = Gg [ln(1 + eCgVG)/Cg]ξ + Ig0    IA = IK − IG

Grid current for the Koren valves uses Koren's own SPICE network: RGI = 2 kΩ in series with a diode (IS = 1 nA, RS = 1 Ω) [2].

The EF86 set [3] is a community fit to the Philips data sheet in Koren's format, not by Koren himself. Its KG2 = 4500 is a value repeated across that library, not a per-valve fit, so I hold the screen at a fixed 100 V and screen current only affects the DC cathode current. 6AN8P (Koren's own small-signal pentode fit) is also in the code as a second pentode reference.

The two 12AX7 models agree to a median of 10% in plate current over the region this stage uses (Vg -3..0 V, Va 80..250 V, Ia(Koren) > 0.1 mA). The 90th percentile is 42%, and they diverge most near cutoff, which is exactly where bias tricks live. That spread is a useful warning: results near cutoff depend on which model and which fit you pick. Dempwolf–Zölzer's set is a fit to one measured valve, and Koren's is a fit to published curves.

3. The stage and how it is solved

B+ → Rp → plate, AC-coupled into RL (the next grid leak). The cathode resistor Rk is fully bypassed, and the input feeds the grid through Rs. Values: B+ = 250 V, Rp = 100 k (22 k for the 12AU7), RL = 1 M, Rs = 33 k, and VG2 = 100 V for the pentode. These are illustrative textbook values, not Culture Vulture values.

DC point: solve Vk = Rk·IK(−Vk, Va) with Va on the DC load line. Dynamic, memoryless transfer (the coupling and bypass capacitors are treated as large, so Vk0 and Va0 hold over a cycle):

vg = vin − Rs IG(vg − Vk0)     (B − Va)/Rp = IP(vg − Vk0, Va − Vk0) + (Va − Va0)/RL     y = Va − Va0

Each equation is monotone in its unknown, so a bracketed Newton–Raphson (bisection fallback) always converges. The tests check it against the small-signal answer −gm(Rp∥RL∥ra) from the model's own derivatives, to within 0.2%.

Bias as a knob. To compare valves fairly I define bias by where the quiescent plate sits, Va0/B+, from hot (0.40) to cold (0.90). For each setting I solve for the Vgk0 and the cathode resistor that produce it, so every bias point is a physically realisable stage. "Drive" is expressed in multiples of A10%, the input amplitude that gives 10% THD at the centre bias (Va0 = 0.55 B+).

The curves show the mechanism directly. Positive input swings drive the plate down toward its knee and into grid conduction (soft, through Rs). Negative swings push toward cutoff. A cold bias brings cutoff close, a hot bias brings the knee close, and only in between are the two clip points roughly symmetric.

4. Harmonics vs drive and bias

At small drive every single-ended stage is H2-dominant, the familiar "valve warmth". As drive rises, H3 grows faster (roughly 3× the slope of H1 in dB versus 2× for H2) and overtakes H2 somewhere between 1× and 2×A10% at centre bias.

What the bias knob does (in this model). At light drive the stage stays even-dominant at any bias. Once drive reaches both clip points, bias decides the balance. There is a fairly narrow "symmetric" bias where H2 cancels and the sound turns odd and harder. Toward cold bias the spectrum swings strongly back to even. Toward hot bias the triodes return to mildly even, but the pentode stays odd-dominant across the range tested. The pentode's symmetric point sits at a hotter bias than the triodes', and at 1× drive it is the most odd-dominant (-12 dB vs -8 to -6 dB). Its plate current barely depends on plate voltage, so its transfer curve stays straighter and then clips more abruptly at both ends. This gives a plausible mechanism for a bias control that steers the character from subtle to harsh. Whether the real unit's bias control works this way is an open question that only measurements of a real unit can answer.

5. Antialiasing on this nonlinearity

Setup: the EF86 stand-in stage at centre bias and 2×A10% drive (1.99 V pk, about 21% THD), sampled at 48 kHz. The stage is tabulated once (4097 points, max error 0.05 mV against the Newton solve, on a swing of about 200 V). Naive, oversampled and ADAA versions all use the same table. For first-order ADAA [5][6], the piecewise-linear table has an exact piecewise-quadratic antiderivative F:

y[n] = (F(x[n]) − F(x[n−1])) / (x[n] − x[n−1]),    falling back to f((x[n] + x[n−1])/2) when |x[n] − x[n−1]| < ε

Metric: input frequencies sit on odd FFT bins (coherent sampling), with a rectangular window. Every true harmonic and every alias then lands on its own bin, so the measurement floor is about -248 dB. I report the energy in non-harmonic bins between 20 Hz and 20 kHz relative to the harmonic energy (lower is better). Oversampling uses scipy's polyphase FIR (Kaiser β=5, 20L+1 taps), and "long FIR" uses Kaiser β=10 with 64L+1 taps.

Solving the stage directly with Newton for every sample cost 9.6 µs per sample in vectorised Python (up to 46 iterations across a block). That is why a memoryless stage should become a table, or a fitted closed form, in the plugin.

Antialiasing takeaways.
  • ADAA1 on its own is cheap (about 7 ns per sample in C), but it only buys 7–10 dB on this curve. It also has a gentle built-in low-pass: H1 drops 1.0 dB at 10 kHz, plus a half-sample delay.
  • 2× oversampling with ADAA1 (-76.9 dB at 5 kHz) beats plain 2× (-59.3 dB) by 18 dB, at roughly the cost of 2× alone.
  • 4× and 8× with scipy's default filter both stop near -87.5 to -88.3 dB at 5 kHz, because the filter's stopband is the limit. The long filter takes 8× to -135.4 dB. So the oversampling filter design matters more than the factor, which matches Kahles et al. [7].
  • At 1 kHz, naive is already at -88 dB and ADAA1 at -95 dB, and every oversampled option is below -137 dB. Aliasing is a high-frequency, high-drive problem.

7. What this means for the plugin, and next steps

  1. Bias belongs in the model, not as an EQ trick. The even/odd balance comes from where the bias sits relative to the two clip points. A plugin "bias" control should move the operating point of a solved stage, or index a family of tables as the demo does.
  2. Core architecture to start from: per stage, a 2-D table f(x, bias) with exact antiderivative, ADAA1 on top of 2× oversampling, and a properly designed half-band or polyphase filter. That is about 50 ns per sample per stage in scalar C before SIMD, so a three-stage stereo chain uses about 1.4% of one core at 48 kHz before any optimisation. Interpolating bias between tables needs smoothing on the bias parameter. ADAA with a time-varying table is a known gotcha: changing F between n−1 and n breaks the difference quotient.
  3. C/C++ details we now know we need: compute F and the difference quotient in double, or rescale, because float32 cancellation hurts when x[n] ≈ x[n−1]. Flush denormals in the FIR states. No allocation on the audio thread, and the tables are built off-thread on parameter change. ADAA's half-sample delay matters if a dry/wet blend is offered.
  4. What the memoryless model misses (the next modelling step): blocking distortion from grid current charging the coupling capacitor, which is audible "sag" and bias shift under heavy drive, the cathode bypass (frequency-dependent gain), Miller capacitance, and inter-stage filtering. Those need a stateful model, either a DK-method state-space or a WDF stage with the valve as the nonlinear root, and stateful ADAA [8] or oversampling.
  5. Data we need: 6AS6 plate curves (including g3 control) to fit a real model in place of the EF86 stand-in, and, most of all, measurements of a real unit: sine sweeps and THD at several drive and bias settings, plus each mode. Without them, "sounds like" claims are off the table.
  6. Verification plan: once a circuit hypothesis exists, run it in ngspice with these same Koren subcircuits and null-test the Python/C++ model against it (frequency response, harmonic profile, transient).
